mcqs.question: What privileges does a script loaded from a vendor's CDN have on your page?
options: Only access to the variables and DOM nodes your code explicitly passes to it
Exactly the same privileges as your own first-party code
Read-only DOM access, with writes restricted to elements it created
The privileges of the vendor's origin, not yours
mcqs.explanation: A script's authority comes from the document that loaded it rather than from where it was fetched, so a vendor script can read the DOM, read storage, and call your API with the user's session exactly as your own code can. There is no partial-trust or read-only mode for script tags — that is precisely why containment has to come from CSP, sandboxing, or keeping it off the page.

mcqs.question: You add `integrity` to a cross-origin script tag and the script stops loading entirely. What is the most likely cause?
options: The hash was generated with sha384 instead of the required sha512
SRI cannot be used with scripts served from a different origin
The `crossorigin="anonymous"` attribute is missing, so the response is opaque and cannot be verified
The browser needs `defer` on any tag carrying an integrity attribute
mcqs.explanation: Without the CORS attribute the browser receives an opaque response it cannot hash, so verification fails and the script is blocked — this is the single most common SRI integration problem. sha384 is a perfectly valid choice, and cross-origin resources are exactly the case SRI was designed for.

mcqs.question: Your bundle includes a malicious transitive npm dependency. Does SRI on your bundle detect it?
options: No — you hash the compromised bundle yourself, so the integrity check passes
Yes — the hash will not match the version published before the compromise
Yes, but only if the dependency was added after the hash was generated
No, because SRI applies only to stylesheets and not to script bundles
mcqs.explanation: SRI verifies that the file delivered matches the file you built, and the poisoned dependency is compiled into that build — so the hash is computed over the malicious artifact and matches perfectly. It answers whether the bytes were tampered with in transit or at the CDN, not whether the source was trustworthy.

mcqs.question: A vendor publishes a legitimately-signed new version of their script that skims form data. Which control still limits the damage?
options: Subresource Integrity, because the hash changed
The `crossorigin` attribute, which restricts what the script may read
A CSP `connect-src` naming only approved hosts, which blocks sending the data out
`npm ci --ignore-scripts`, which blocks the malicious lifecycle hook
mcqs.explanation: SRI checks identity, not intent — a legitimately published update simply gets a new hash, and once you update it the check passes. Exfiltration still has to leave the browser, so a tight `connect-src` is the chokepoint every variant of this attack must pass through, and it generates a violation report as a bonus.

mcqs.question: Why is a marketing tag manager often the least-governed deployment path in a company?
options: Tag managers execute scripts in a sandboxed context outside normal review
Anyone with container access can push arbitrary JavaScript to production, bypassing code review and CI
Tags run only after page load, so they fall outside the security perimeter
Tag managers are hosted by the vendor, so the vendor is accountable for the code
mcqs.explanation: A tag container is a remote code execution channel by design: it publishes JavaScript straight to production without passing through code review, CI, or the release process, and the containers it loads often pull in further vendors nobody inventoried. Nothing about it is sandboxed, and running after load places it fully inside your origin.
